title: National Health Amendment (Pharmaceutical Benefits—Budget and Other Measures) Bill 2017
short_title: National Health Amendment (Pharmaceutical Benefits—Budget and Other Measures) Bill 2017

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill changes how the price of certain medicines on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme is reduced over time.
It would extend and add new price reductions for single-brand drugs, raise the reduction for the first new brand, and let the Minister adjust reductions in some cases.
The bill also removes the clauses that would end the pharmacy location rules and the authority that supports them in 2020, and makes small fixes to price disclosure.
changes: The five per cent price cut for drugs listed five years is extended to 2022.
A one-off ten per cent cut applies in June 2018 to drugs listed ten to fifteen years, and further cuts apply in April 2019, 2020, and 2021.
Drugs listed fifteen years or more get a one-off ten per cent cut then five per cent, totalling 14.5 per cent.
The cut for the first new brand rises from 16 to 25 per cent from October 2018, then returns to 16 per cent in July 2022.
The Minister can reduce or waive a price cut if the medicine already had cuts since January 2016.
The sunset clauses for the pharmacy authority and location rules are removed.
summary.affected: Drug companies, pharmacies, and the Australian Community Pharmacy Authority.

divisions.question: The majority voted in favour of a motion that part 1 of schedule 5 *stand as printed.* This is parliamentary jargon for leaving that part unchanged. This vote was put after NSW Senator David Leyonhjelm (Liberal Democratic Party) [proposed that](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2018-02-13.7.1) the part be opposed. Senator Leyonhjelm [explained that](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2018-02-13.11.1): > *What my amendment [to oppose this part] would do would be to remove something which is quite unnecessary in this bill we are considering. The rest of the bill is fine, but this rather sneaky little provision removes the June 2020 sunset clause that regulates the location of pharmacies and establishes whether an application to establish one can be granted.* ### What is part 1, schedule 5? > *Part 1 — Australian Community Pharmacy Authority* > > *National Health Act 1953* > > *1 Subsection 90(3C)* > > *Repeal the subsection.* > > *2 Section 99Y* > > *Repeal the section.*

speeches.speaker: Greg Hunt
speeches.brief: The bill amends the National Health Act to implement 2017 budget measures negotiated with Medicines Australia, the Generic and Biosimilar Medicines Association, and the Pharmacy Guild, generating $1.3 billion in PBS savings over four years and $1.8 billion over five years, while extending anniversary price reductions, increasing the first new brand price reduction from 16% to 25%, adjusting price disclosure thresholds, and preserving pharmacy location rules.

speeches.speaker: Catherine King
speeches.brief: Labor supported the bill, which extends price disclosure reforms and introduces new price reductions for PBS medicines, but questioned whether the government had already spent the $1.8 billion in savings it claims the bill will deliver. The party also noted that the government has listed only a fraction of the $20 billion in PBS savings achieved under Labor's reforms.

speeches.speaker: Mike Freelander
speeches.brief: Labor will not oppose the National Health Amendment (Pharmaceutical Benefits—Budget and Other Measures) Bill 2017, which increases the price reduction for competing brands from 16% to 25% and implements 2017-18 budget PBS measures; the speaker welcomed consumer price cuts and reinvestment in new listings but raised concerns about transparency, whether savings will cover future drug costs, and the repeal of the pharmacy location sunset clause, while urging a national real-time prescription monitoring system.

speeches.speaker: Greg Hunt
speeches.brief: The speaker tabled an addendum and a correction to the explanatory memorandum for the National Health Amendment (Pharmaceutical Benefits—Budget and Other Measures) Bill 2017, and announced $16 million for the first national real-time prescription monitoring service. He detailed agreements with Medicines Australia, the Generic and Biosimilar Medicines Association, and the Pharmacy Guild of Australia, along with PBS reinvestments including $1.1 billion for Opdivo, $378.5 million for Stelara, and $466 million for Ibrutinib.
